FALSE_POSITIVE on Law 60 as written. The finding asserts these calls are "used in async functions" and that they are in "async contexts", but every single cited line sits in a plain `def`. I verified this by AST rather than by grep, which is the check the finding skipped.
Each site is correct as written, and "fixing" any of them would be a regression:
  - jobs/ai_tasks.py: the asyncio.run() calls are inside SYNC Celery task bodies. A Celery worker task owning its own event loop via asyncio.run() is the standard, correct pattern - calling it from a coroutine would be the error.
  - circuit_breaker.call()/retry() are deliberate SYNC facades that wrap the async _async_wrapper/_async_retry and bridge them with asyncio.run(). That is a designed sync-over-async API, and sync is required because the callers include sync service code.

  - rate_limit_middleware.py:73 is inside _cleanup_memory_store, which is the target of a daemon threading.Thread started at module import. A dedicated background thread is exactly where a blocking sleep belongs.
The codebase is in fact exemplary on Law 60: every blocking-style call that does live inside a coroutine uses `await asyncio.sleep(...)`.
SEPARATE GENUINE DEFECT surfaced and routed to coverage_gaps (NOT filed as a finding here, per contract §6): circuit_breaker.retry() - the SYNC wrapper - is invoked from 5 async functions at backend/domains/country/services/research/country_auto_populate.py:421, 501, 551, 593, 621. asyncio.run() from inside a running loop raises RuntimeError, so those five endpoints are broken.    total relationship() calls: 375

   top files: hr/models/employee_models.py 44, comms/models/communication.py 27, country/models/countries.py 21, country/models/country_enhancements.py 21, comms/models/chat.py 19, logistics/models/logistics_entities.py 17, security/models/fraud.py 15, catalog/models/products.py 14

  domains/accounts/models/core.py       relationship("User", back_populates="addresses")
  domains/accounts/models/onboarding.py  relationship("User")
  domains/accounts/models/onboarding.py  relationship("OnboardingStep", back_populates="pipeline", cascade="all, delete-orphan")
§12 Law 45: "All relationships declare lazy=selectin or joined. Default lazy=select FORBIDDEN." 293 of 375 (78%) rely on the forbidden default.

COMPLIANCE ATTESTATION THAT NO LONGER HOLDS - returned REAL, and the single most under-reported finding in the packet.
The row asserts flat compliance. In fact 293 of 375 relationship() declarations in backend/domains have no lazy= argument at all and so fall back to SQLAlchemy's default lazy="select" - the exact thing Law 45 forbids - across 38 files. The claim is not a near-miss; it is inverted.
WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE COUNT SUGGESTS: Law 45 is the codebase's own articulation of the N+1 problem, and its Why column names the consequence explicitly ("N+1 queries bring the database to its knees at 100K+ users"). 293 implicitly lazy relationships is the textbook mechanism for exactly that failure, and ARCH §3 lists "MAU > 100,000" as a scale trigger. The audit not only missed it, it certified the opposite.
SCOPE NOTE, stated honestly: some of these relationships are plausibly never traversed (unused joins cost nothing), and some back_populates pairs are bidirectional by necessity. The correct fix is therefore not a blind sed - it is to set lazy="selectin" on the relationships that are actually navigated and to leave the rest explicit, which is also what makes the residual meaningful. A baseline-gated test (the pattern this repo already uses in _router_logic_baseline.txt) is the right mechanism.
No BENCHMARK MISMATCH: the row Target "No N+1 queries" matches §12 Law 45 exactly. This is a compliance regression the dimension file should be amended to record.

  domains/accounts/models/user.py:44-48
      referred_by_user_id = Column(

          ForeignKey("accounts.users.id", ondelete="SET NULL"),

      )
  domains/accounts/models/mfa_factor.py:36-40
      user_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey("accounts.users.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), nullable=False)   <- no index=
  domains/accounts/models/password_history.py:25, domains/accounts/models/refresh_token_family.py:64

verdicts.notes:
COMPLIANCE ATTESTATION THAT NO LONGER HOLDS - returned REAL.
24 foreign-key columns are declared without an index. The clearest is domains/accounts/models/user.py:44 referred_by_user_id, and the pattern repeats through that file at lines 99, 133, 163, 193, 222 and 251, plus mfa_factor.py:36, password_history.py:25 and refresh_token_family.py:64.
I checked the obvious false-positive source before reporting: these are not compensated by an Index(...) or ix_* assignment in the same class, which is the usual reason a naive scan over-reports. The 24 are genuine.
PRACTICAL IMPACT worth naming for the resolver: the accounts.user table is the most frequently joined table in the platform (referrals, MFA factors, password history, token families, orders, and 6+ further FKs all point at it), and PostgreSQL does not auto-index the referencing side of a foreign key. Each of these is a sequential scan waiting for the table to grow past the buffer cache. The Why column of Law 53 says exactly this.
Cheap, mechanical, and safe to fix: add index=True (or an explicit Index) to the 24 columns. No migration is needed for the declaration change, though index=True on a mapped column will generate one via Alembic.
No BENCHMARK MISMATCH: the row Target matches §12 Law 53 exactly.
